subject: Anatomy
summary: The biceps brachii is a two‑headed muscle that flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm. Its long head forms part of the shoulder joint capsule, while the short head lies in the cubital fossa. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose common injuries and guide surgical approaches.

sections.p: The biceps brachii is a superficial muscle of the upper arm, important for elbow flexion and forearm supination. It has two heads that insert on the radial tuberosity and the bicipital aponeurosis.

The long head originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and travels through the bicipital groove. The short head originates from the coracoid process. Both heads converge into a single tendon.
The long head lies within the bicipital groove, protected by the intertubercular sulcus. The short head lies in the cubital fossa, adjacent to the brachial artery and median nerve.
Supplied by the musculocutaneous artery (branch of the lateral thoracic artery) and the radial recurrent artery.
Primary actions are elbow flexion and forearm supination. It also stabilises the shoulder joint during overhead activities.
Common injuries include tendinopathy, subluxation of the long head, and distal biceps rupture. In low‑resource settings, infections or trauma may lead to tendon rupture.

t.b: Detects tendon tears and inflammation; a high signal in the tendon indicates tendinopathy or partial tear.
Shows bone alignment; a distal radius fracture may coexist with biceps injury.
Evaluates tendon integrity when MRI is unavailable; a hypoechoic area suggests rupture.

sections.p: Remember the long head contributes to the anastomosis of the shoulder joint capsule and that the tendon of the biceps lies in the cubital fossa.
b: Long head part of shoulder capsule anastomosis

whenToSeekHelp: Severe elbow pain with inability to supinate, sudden loss of forearm function, or a visible deformity at the elbow

faq.a: Overuse, repetitive overhead activities, or poor biomechanics. Infections like TB can also affect the tendon in endemic areas.

faq.q: How is a distal biceps rupture treated?
faq.a: Surgical repair is preferred for full ruptures; conservative management is for partial tears or low-demand patients.

faq.q: Can a biceps injury mimic a nerve problem?
faq.a: Yes, a long head subluxation can compress the median nerve, causing numbness in the hand.

exam: Explain the anatomical pathway of the long head of the biceps and its clinical significance.
Describe the management steps for a distal biceps rupture in a low‑resource setting.
Identify the nerve supply to the biceps and explain how injury to this nerve would present clinically.
